title: The Fast and the Furious: Tokyo Drift
full_review:
A strong contender for most irresponsible movie of the year, "The Fast and the Furious: Tokyo Drift" (Universal), is little more than a glossy 98-minute commercial for reckless driving. The loud and the ludicrous is more like it.

Third in the adrenaline-charged series -- the first without Paul Walker behind the wheel -- the film stars Lucas Black as Sean Boswell, a drag-racing rebel, who is sent to live with his estranged Navy dad (Brian Goodman) in Japan.

There he befriends fellow American, Twinkie (recording artist Bow Wow), who introduces him to Tokyo's underground "drift racing" scene, referring to the driving technique of gliding around hairpin turns at breakneck speed. Sean's outsider status makes him a target for the mob-connected champ, D.K. (Brian Tee). The animosity heats up when Sean flirts with D.K.'s girlfriend, Neela (Nathalie Kelley) -- whose presence, like the rest of the women in the film, is mere window dressing. (In the opening scene, a high school student offers herself as a trophy to the winner of a race.)

Director Justin Lin delivers more of the same high-octane -- tedious -- race sequences, macho posturing and sexist images but, as before, there's little plot under the film's flashy hood. By this third lap, the franchise is running on fumes.

Much of action occurs in grungy garages, and the film never really takes advantage of the Tokyo backdrop apart from a few neon-lit night shots.

Black's performance lit up "Friday Night Lights," but here he's reduced to a crash-test dummy.

Late in the film, there is a scene in which D.K. pursues Sean and another racer (Sung Kang) through a crowded intersection. Given the film's PG-13 rating, what's troubling is that impressionable young viewers may think such sequences "cool." By that point, however, most thinking adults will likely find their attention "drifting" to the nearest exit.

The film contains much hazardous and illegal behavior involving teens, some violence, objectification of women, several implied sexual situations including same-sex kissing, suggestive wardrobe and dancing, and scattered crude language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
